name: Embrace
label: Dischord
lede: Nine shows in under a year, one album released after the band was already gone, and the moment Ian MacKaye slowed hardcore down to hear what else it could say.

eras.title: Minor Threat's singer, The Faith's band
eras.text: Two years after Minor Threat, Ian MacKaye wanted out of the violence that had swallowed hardcore shows, not out of punk. Embrace kept the fire but slowed the tempo, and turned the songs toward greed, self-delusion and the scene itself, right as Revolution Summer was remaking D.C.

years.h: MacKaye plus three-quarters of The Faith
years.p: [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] joins [[Michael Hampton|4ed83c42-6348-4368-903e-9116bfa49b8e]], [[Chris Bald|0838359b-95a7-48e9-a9f6-0e8f40bb34d2]] and [[Ivor Hanson|a17981f7-ab3d-46dc-859a-582ac894cb20]], three ex-members of [[The Faith|f735a867-9a16-451f-8f83-669ed42e2574]], the band his brother [[Alec MacKaye|bb05a948-ea44-4c9b-9d19-2a48f757ca22]] had fronted. Hampton and Hanson go back even further, to [[State of Alert|e54cb250-3502-4c32-9482-70488bd9a8cb]].

years.cap: Embrace at Food for Thought, July 1985: Chris Bald, Ian MacKaye, Mike Hampton
years.h: First show: Food for Thought, Dupont Circle
years.p: Embrace debut at the Dupont Circle venue in the middle of Revolution Summer. MacKaye's new band is slower, more melodic and more inward than anything he'd fronted before.
years.xp:
AllMusic's line on them: the fire and passion of hardcore, albeit slower and more heartfelt. Dischord describes small rooms and a personal, introspective take on punk rock.

Across town, [[Rites of Spring|b2ff1a6d-9198-4646-b068-8965242d245b]] were pulling in the same direction. Between the two bands, D.C. hardcore was learning a new register.

years.h: Into Inner Ear with Don Zientara
years.p: Sessions for the album begin at [[Don Zientara|a495882b-4585-4295-9269-e30c63f279fe]]'s Inner Ear studio in Arlington, Virginia. They'll run on and off into February.

years.h: The night "emocore" was born, by one account
years.p: Embrace share a bill with [[Dag Nasty|4709dd69-1034-4634-9e88-d1099453b192]] and Rites of Spring. Dag Nasty guitarist [[Brian Baker|1fd36abf-e43c-4b01-820b-d7280cc27ea5]], MacKaye's old Minor Threat bandmate, says he made up "emocore" that night to mock the Rites of Spring set. That's his own account, told to Parade in 2025.

eras.title: Nine shows and out
eras.text: Embrace finished their record and then simply stopped. By spring MacKaye was in London recording with his old Minor Threat drummer, Hampton was in a new band with three ex-Rites of Spring members, and the album sat waiting.

years.h: The sessions wrap, with a guest guitarist
years.p: Fourteen songs in the can. [[Eddie Janney|323dd1dd-23e4-45ce-9aa9-c5492096d604]] of Rites of Spring plays guitar on one track and shares the production credit with the band and MacKaye.
Show number nine is the end. AllMusic's word for the breakup: unceremonious. No farewell, just done.
years.xp: The four scattered fast. Hampton went to [[One Last Wish|94f18045-7fe2-41df-bf24-0bed21c88eb8]], Bald to [[Ignition|3cb2b7d6-1f0b-4ac5-b67f-52132f3d3b61]], and Hanson would reunite with Hampton in Manifesto. MacKaye tried a few things before landing on Fugazi.

years.p: MacKaye and [[Jeff Nelson|51f7994c-949d-4dbe-89eb-2c33f42a5620]] record four songs at Southern Records' Wood Green studio in England and name the project after the weekend. Dischord calls it the last time the two recorded music together.

years.h: Hampton joins three ex-Rites of Spring
years.p: Guy Picciotto, Eddie Janney and Brendan Canty start One Last Wish with Hampton on guitar.

years.h: Egg Hunt tries to become a band
years.p: MacKaye and Nelson try to build a full lineup with ex-members of [[Gray Matter|c9065214-ba09-4c2c-b341-35713b702264]]. In Dischord's words, it wasn't meant to be.

years.big: The scene had a new name for what they did. He didn't want it.
years.h: A new word, and MacKaye's verdict on it
years.p: Fans and zines started calling Embrace and Rites of Spring "emocore." In 1986, MacKaye was blunt about it.
years.xp: For MacKaye the point had been to strip away hardcore's posturing, not to start a subgenre. The label stuck anyway and outlived both bands by decades.

eras.title: The record outlives the band
eras.text: The album came out more than a year after the last show, from a band that no longer existed. By then its singer had a new group that would make Embrace's slower, searching sound the starting point for something much bigger.

years.p: Fourteen songs, about 33 minutes. Critics singled out MacKaye's cutting lyrics and the muscle of the playing. Critic Mark Jenkins heard sermons against greed, delusion and self-destruction, and credited Bald with much of the words.
years.xp:
Trouser Press argued the strong, muscular instrumentals turned an okay mid-tempo punk LP into a great one.

Songs like Money and Last Song pointed straight at where MacKaye was headed next.

years.h: MacKaye's next band plays its first show
years.p: [[Fugazi|233fc3f3-6de2-465c-985e-e721dbabbace]] debut at the Wilson Center. Brendan Canty is on drums, and Guy Picciotto is singing with them within weeks: two of the Rites of Spring players Embrace had shared those 1985 bills with.
The guitarist and drummer who went back to State of Alert reunite in Manifesto.

eras.title: Other bands' Embrace
eras.text: Embrace never reunited, but the record kept getting remade, remastered and covered. A younger generation of hardcore and pop-punk bands paid it back in the most D.C. way possible: a benefit.

years.h: On CD, with a new cover
years.p: The album arrives on CD and cassette with alternate cover art.

years.h: A tribute that pays for shelter beds
years.p: Trustkill Records releases Land of Greed... World of Need, with [[Avail|d67ff511-57b8-4d02-94d3-6c6a331c2ae4]], [[Rancid|24f8d8a5-269b-475c-a1cb-792990b0b2ee]] and [[Lifetime|c9329809-8510-45b9-9202-5640398ddaee]] among the bands covering Embrace. Proceeds go to homeless shelters.
Chad Clark remasters the album at Silver Sonya, and alternate versions of Money and Dance of Days are added.
After a red vinyl pressing in 2008, the LP is remastered by Jason Ward at Chicago Mastering Service.
